title: Constructed, Not Sampled: Identification in Recorded Data
content: Statistical analysis usually begins from recorded values treated as draws from a distribution. Those values acquired their numerical form through processes—choice of unit, rounding and coding, biological, arithmetic and institutional constraints, composition from other quantities, aggregation and ordering—that the abstraction X1, . . . , Xn ∼ F leaves implicit. This article develops a construction-aware identification framework for recorded numerical data. An upstream state Z passes through a construction map indexed by a regime M to give the recorded value X, which an analyst transforms into a representation P(X) on which a diagnostic is computed. The framework makes the construction regime an explicit inferential target alongside the upstream state and shows that the two identification problems can move in opposite directions: a rounding rule can be ignorable for inference about a mean and yet identifiable from terminal digits. It places the analyst’s representation on the same chain as the recording process, so that a distinction the recorded values carry can be destroyed before any diagnostic is computed. Formal results characterize when construction regimes are observationally distinguishable from recorded values, when support alone can exclude a regime, and when a representation preserves or destroys that distinction. A locating vocabulary—unitization, quantization, constraint, composition, aggregation—says where numerical structure entered a record, and worked cases from temperature archives, survey blood pressure, the genetic code, check digits, marathon qualifying standards, seawater sound speed, tide gauges and federal spending records show the framework operating in each class. The practical consequence is a change in what a numerical diagnostic reports: not an anomaly flag, but whether the construction regime is identified, partially identified, excluded, or not identified by the information at hand.
